claims.text: The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy and all compared equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets have single-phase FCC microstructures after identical thermomechanical processing.
Differences in deformation and failure behavior among these alloys are caused by variations in stacking-fault energy.
Differences in deformation and failure behavior among these alloys are caused by differences in defect evolution.
The presence or absence of Mn mediates the proposed stacking-fault-energy and defect-evolution differences.
Mn alters local electronic and magnetic interactions in the quinary alloy.
Mn-induced electronic and magnetic interactions increase the effective stacking-fault energy of the quinary alloy.
Higher stacking-fault energy suppresses deformation twinning.
Deformation of the quinary alloy is predominantly dislocation-controlled under the stated conditions.
Reduction or absence of Mn in the lower-component alloys decreases their stacking-fault energy relative to the quinary alloy.
Lower stacking-fault energy facilitates stacking-fault formation and deformation twinning.
The quaternary and ternary alloys begin twinning earlier and form twins more prolifically than the quinary alloy.
Changes in twinning and dislocation-slip dynamics alter strain hardening and ductility.
All tested quaternary and ternary subsets will develop a higher density of deformation twins than the quinary baseline.
The quaternary and ternary subsets will exhibit dislocation-density or diffraction-profile evolution different from the quinary baseline.
The altered defect evolution will produce modified strain-hardening behavior and ductility relative to the quinary baseline.
The proposed mechanism is applicable at room temperature under controlled-rate uniaxial tensile loading of thermomechanically processed single-phase FCC samples.

contradictions.description: The mechanism attributes lower stacking-fault energy and enhanced twinning primarily to reduction or absence of Mn, but the prediction is applied to every quaternary and ternary subset. Some equiatomic subsets can retain Mn, so constituent-count reduction does not necessarily constitute Mn removal or reduction.
